Country.evidence_source: Many of the participants came of age during times when the Royal Mounted Canadian Police and other Canadian police surveilled gay citizens and raided gay bars and bathhouses (Gollom, 2016; Kinsman & Gentile, 2010), and during the early years of the AIDS epidemic, when AIDS diagnoses or deaths "outed" previously closeted gay men (Crimp, 1992; Figure 1).

Population.evidence_source: The prominence of this narrative in interviews with gay men who have attempted suicide suggests it should continue to be explored by mental health professionals.

Type.evidence_source: Several participants arrived at the interviews—notably responding to our study pitch regarding a statistical association between sexuality and suicide assuming that we perceived suicide attempts to be in direct response to antigay stigma (e.g., persecution or bullying, as exhibited in Turing's and Lucas's stories).

Area.evidence_source: The pride narrative resists any notion of a causal relationship between sexual orientation and suicide and, thus, can be a powerful form of coping, as it was for this participant. It should be noted, however, that the pride narrative is also rigid. Those who cannot comply with it are "at risk" for suicide, by failing to achieve the supportive connections offered by gay community socialization, like that described by the participant quoted earlier (Cover & Prosser, 2013).
